lead: A real engine is messy: fuel burns, the gas changes its make-up and heat leaks through the walls. An air standard cycle replaces all of that by a fixed mass of air that goes through a few simple, reversible processes and returns to its starting state. It gives the best efficiency an engine of that shape could reach. Every gas cycle in this unit starts from these assumptions; the Carnot cycle is the limit.
prereq: You need the ideal gas equation, the isentropic relation pv<sup>γ</sup> = constant and the heat transfer formulas of the topic Non-flow processes: isothermal, adiabatic, polytropic. Carnot's theorem comes from the topic Carnot cycle and Carnot's theorem.

blocks.text: An air standard analysis rests on four assumptions.

items: Working fluid. A fixed mass of air is the working fluid all through the cycle. Air is an ideal gas, pv = RT, with R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.

Heat instead of combustion. Burning fuel is replaced by heat added from an outside hot source. The exhaust and suction strokes are replaced by heat rejected to an outside cold sink, so the same air returns to state 1 and the cycle is closed.
Reversible processes. Every process is internally reversible. Compression and expansion are frictionless and adiabatic, so they are isentropic.

Constant specific heats. cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and γ = cp/cv = 1.4, the values for air near room temperature. With these room values the analysis is often called the cold air standard.

blocks.text: With these four, the cycle is a loop on the p-v and T-s diagrams, and the heat and work of each process follow from first-law formulas. The figure of merit is the air standard efficiency:

Here wnet is the net work per kg of air in one cycle, qin is the heat added and qout the heat rejected, all in kJ/kg. It depends only on the shape and ratios of the cycle; a real engine reaches well below it. The ratio of the actual thermal efficiency to the air standard efficiency is called the relative efficiency (some syllabi say efficiency ratio).

sections.h3: Process relations used in every gas cycle

blocks.text: Four kinds of process build all the cycles of this unit. Per kg of air, with temperatures in kelvin:

items: Isentropic (reversible adiabatic): pvγ = constant, T₂/T₁ = (v₁/v₂)γ−1 = (p₂/p₁)(γ−1)/γ. No heat; work = cv(T₁ − T₂) in a closed system.
Constant volume: p/T = constant. Heat q = cv(T₂ − T₁); no displacement work.
Constant pressure: v/T = constant. Heat q = cp(T₂ − T₁); work = p(v₂ − v₁).
Isothermal: pv = constant. Heat = work = RT ln(v₂/v₁); entropy change Δs = R ln(v₂/v₁).

blocks.text: On a T-s diagram an isentropic process is a vertical line and an isothermal process a horizontal line. A constant-volume line rises more steeply than a constant-pressure line through the same point, because its slope is T/c<sub>v</sub> and c<sub>v</sub> is smaller than c<sub>p</sub>. That one fact explains most of the comparisons between cycles later in the unit.

sections.h3: The Carnot cycle as the reference

blocks.text: The Carnot gas cycle takes in all its heat at the highest temperature T<sub>H</sub> and rejects all of it at the lowest temperature T<sub>L</sub>. With state 1 the start of compression, its four processes are:

items: 1→2 isentropic compression from T<sub>L</sub> to T<sub>H</sub>.
2→3 isothermal expansion at T<sub>H</sub>; heat q<sub>in</sub> = RT<sub>H</sub> ln(v₃/v₂) is taken in.
3→4 isentropic expansion from T<sub>H</sub> back to T<sub>L</sub>.
4→1 isothermal compression at T<sub>L</sub>; heat q<sub>out</sub> = RT<sub>L</sub> ln(v₄/v₁) is rejected.

blocks.text: The two isentropic steps have the same temperature ratio, so v₄/v₁ = v₃/v₂ and the logarithms cancel in q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>. On the T-s diagram the cycle is a rectangle, and

No engine between the same two temperatures can beat it (Carnot's theorem), yet no engine runs on it, for three reasons. Isothermal heat transfer needs the gas to move slowly, which a piston at thousands of revolutions per minute cannot allow. The isentropic steps need a very large volume ratio and pressure ratio, so the cylinder is long and heavy for the work it gives. And the net work is a small difference between large positive and negative works, so friction in a real machine eats most of it. Two numbers measure this: the work ratio (net work divided by the positive work) and the mean effective pressure, defined in the chapter Air standard efficiency, mean effective pressure, comparison. Both are very low for the Carnot cycle, as the worked example shows.

examples.question: An air standard Carnot cycle works between 300 K and 900 K. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 300 K. During heat addition the volume doubles (v₃/v₂ = 2). Take R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find the pressure and specific volume at each state, the heat added, the net work, the efficiency, the work ratio and the mean effective pressure.
steps: State 1: v₁ = RT₁/p₁ = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg (p in kPa).
Isentropic 1→2: v₁/v₂ = (T₂/T₁)<sup>1/(γ−1)</sup> = 3<sup>2.5</sup> = 15.59, so v₂ = 0.861/15.59 = 0.0552 m³/kg. p₂ = p₁(T₂/T₁)<sup>γ/(γ−1)</sup> = 1 × 3<sup>3.5</sup> = 46.77 bar.
Isothermal 2→3: v₃ = 2v₂ = 0.1105 m³/kg; p₃ = p₂/2 = 23.38 bar.
Isentropic 3→4: the temperature ratio is again 3, so v₄ = 15.59 × v₃ = 1.722 m³/kg and p₄ = 23.38/46.77 = 0.50 bar. Check: v₄/v₁ = 2 = v₃/v₂.
Heat added: q<sub>in</sub> = RT<sub>H</sub> ln 2 = 0.287 × 900 × 0.6931 = 179.0 kJ/kg. Heat rejected: q<sub>out</sub> = 0.287 × 300 × 0.6931 = 59.7 kJ/kg.
Net work: w<sub>net</sub> = 179.0 − 59.7 = 119.4 kJ/kg. Efficiency: η = 119.4/179.0 = 0.667, the same as 1 − 300/900.
Positive work: 179.0 (isothermal) + c<sub>v</sub>(900 − 300) = 430.8 (isentropic), total 609.8 kJ/kg. Work ratio = 119.4/609.8 = 0.196.
Mean effective pressure = w<sub>net</sub>/(v<sub>max</sub> − v<sub>min</sub>) = 119.4/(1.722 − 0.0552) = 71.6 kPa = 0.716 bar.
examples.answer: p₂ = 46.77 bar, p₃ = 23.38 bar, p₄ = 0.50 bar; v₁ = 0.861, v₂ = 0.0552, v₃ = 0.1105, v₄ = 1.722 m³/kg; q<sub>in</sub> = 179.0 kJ/kg, w<sub>net</sub> = 119.4 kJ/kg, η = 66.7%, work ratio 0.196, MEP 0.716 bar. The cycle needs a pressure ratio of about 94 and a volume ratio of about 31 to give a mean pressure below 1 bar: that is why no engine runs on it.

traps: Temperatures in T₂/T₁ = (v₁/v₂)<sup>γ−1</sup> and in 1 − T<sub>L</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> must be in kelvin. Writing 1 − 27/627 instead of 1 − 300/900 gives 95.7% instead of 66.7%.

The air standard efficiency is not the efficiency of the real engine. It is an upper limit for that cycle shape; the real value is lower because of friction, heat loss, variable specific heats and incomplete burning.
The Carnot efficiency does not depend on the working fluid or on the volume ratio during heat addition. Only T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>L</sub> appear.
In the isothermal steps heat equals work, q = RT ln(v₂/v₁). Students often write c<sub>v</sub>ΔT, which is zero there.
A favourite question: "Why is the Carnot cycle not used in practice?" Answer with the low work ratio, the low mean effective pressure and the impossibility of fast isothermal heat transfer.

quiz.q: State the four air standard assumptions.
quiz.a: A fixed mass of air as an ideal gas; combustion and exhaust replaced by heat added from a source and heat rejected to a sink (closed cycle); all processes internally reversible; constant specific heats (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4).

quiz.q: Why does a constant-volume line rise more steeply than a constant-pressure line on a T-s diagram?
quiz.a: Along a constant-volume line ds = c<sub>v</sub> dT/T, so the slope dT/ds = T/c<sub>v</sub>. Along a constant-pressure line the slope is T/c<sub>p</sub>. Since c<sub>v</sub> < c<sub>p</sub>, the constant-volume slope is larger.

quiz.q: Give two reasons why the Carnot cycle is not used for a real engine.
quiz.a: Isothermal heat transfer needs very slow processes, impossible at engine speeds. The cycle needs huge pressure and volume ratios for a small net work, so its work ratio and mean effective pressure are very low and friction would eat most of the output.

quiz.q: A Carnot engine works between 1000 K and 300 K and takes in 200 kJ/kg of heat. Find its efficiency, net work and heat rejected.
In the worked example the volume ratio during heat addition is raised from 2 to 3. Find the new heat added and net work.
In the worked example, the work ratio is 0.196. Suppose friction takes 10% of the positive work. What happens to the net output?
quiz.a: Friction takes 0.10 × 609.8 = 61.0 kJ/kg, so the net output falls from 119.4 to 58.4 kJ/kg, about half. A cycle with a low work ratio loses a large share of its output to small losses.

beyond: Engine designers today go well past the air standard model. Engine simulation codes solve the cycle with temperature-dependent properties, a burn-rate model of the heat release and heat loss to the walls. Thermodynamics texts treat the step between the two models as the fuel-air cycle and the actual cycle. To go further, search for "fuel-air cycle", "variable specific heats air cycle" and "engine cycle simulation".

figure.caption: The worked example’s Carnot cycle between 300 K and 900 K. On the T-s diagram it is a rectangle, and the shaded upper part is the net work; on the p-v diagram the same work is a thin sliver that needs a pressure ratio of 94, which is why its mean effective pressure is so low.
